extracted.subtask_description: Contemporary newspaper coverage and commentary of World War II military, diplomatic, and legal developments, including reportage of battles, strategic analysis, and references to international law. Aimed at informing the general public about events and official positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hague Convention (1899) rules on POW labor
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Hague convention of 1899 provides that prisoners of war may be used as workers provided their tasks have nothing to do with military operations, and that they shall be paid at the same rate as troops of the country into whose hands they have fallen.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal standard cited for when and how prisoners of war may be employed: tasks must be non-military and prisoners must receive pay equivalent to that paid troops of the detaining country. Context: reported as a counterpoint to Japanese moves or reports that prisoners were being put to work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation to abide by the Geneva Convention (conduct of war)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted stance: “Abide by the Geneva Convention governing the conduct’ of war" and the declaration that “we expect our enemies to do the same.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expresses the normative expectation and diplomatic claim that belligerents should follow Geneva Convention protections for combatants, civilians, and prisoners; used to rebut accusations of inhumanity and to assert moral/legal high ground in wartime reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of temporary restraints during prisoner transport
rubrics_metrics.description: The article reports the view that temporary measures — e.g., shackling between the time prisoners came off the boats and the time they reached concentration points — "was no violation of the Geneva convention, but only a matter of guaranteeing security during transportation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes brief security restraints in transit (treated as lawful security measures) from wholesale or prolonged mistreatment; context includes discussion of specific incidents (Dieppe captives) and contrasting German wholesale shackling practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: International accountability for wartime atrocities
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported propaganda/official claim: “The day will come _ eventually when those responsible will be called to account for their actions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement of principle used in diplomatic and propaganda contexts — asserts future legal or moral accountability for alleged violations of humanitarian law. Appears as threat/justification in Axis/Vichy commentary and Allied responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for devastating aerial preparation before amphibious invasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument in commentary: “Only by a devastating aerial preparation can the ground be cleared-for invasion... To attempt to land an army without this would be mass murder... The bomber command works so quickly... It takes the efforts of all services, but it's bombers that can do this particular job for us.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic criterion for successful large-scale amphibious operations: substantial, sustained strategic bombing to degrade enemy industry, transport, and defensive capacity before landing troops. Guidance includes urgent reinforcement of bomber forces and use of air power to render invasion feasible and reduce casualties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus targets for strategic bombing: vital industry and transport hubs
rubrics_metrics.description: Commentary asserts there are “less than 200 prime targets for our combined air forces to destroy” and that “the destruction of 40 of the most vital would knock his hopes into a cocked hat.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive targeting principle: concentrate air effort on a relatively small set of critical industrial, manufacturing, and transport facilities (examples cited: Renault works in Paris) to maximize strategic effect; implies prioritization and economy of effort in strategic bombing campaigns.
